about: Debrief's first-use walkthroughs (CAP-25): the one source of their text for VS Code's Get Started page (package.json contributes.walkthroughs, written from this file by scripts/walkthroughs.mjs) and the playground's Walkthroughs panel. Each step is ticked when the analyst does it: its event is sent by the host when the action succeeds. Text follows the style guide's language section; text, keys and where are shared, the vscode and play parts say only what differs.

tours.title: Open and explore a serial
tours.description: Serial 1 of the sample exercise: move through time, select tracks, compare them in the Tote and read the narrative in the Timeline. About 8 minutes.

steps.title: Open a copy of serial 1
steps.text: Serial 1 of the sample exercise, 15 Jun 2023 from 08:00Z to 12:00Z: BLUE ONE gains RED ONE, a submarine, among merchant traffic east of Chesapeake Bay. You work on a copy, titled *Serial 1: Open and explore a serial*, so the sample itself never changes.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the button and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: The copy goes into a catalogue of its own, *Walkthrough: Open and explore a serial*, in Catalogues.

play.where: The copy is added to the plots under *Plot*, in the top bar.

steps.alt: The map of serial 1: BLUE ONE in blue and RED ONE in red among grey merchant tracks.

steps.title: Move current time
steps.text: Drag **Current time** in the time controller. Each track's position at that time is marked on the map with a square in its colour. **▶** plays; at 60× a minute of the exercise passes each second. The two handles of **Time window** narrow what is drawn in full.
steps.keys: `Tab` to **Current time**; `←` and `→` step it, `Page Up` and `Page Down` step further, `Home` and `End` go to the window's ends. `Space` plays and pauses.

vscode.where: The time controller is **Time**, at the top of the Debrief sidebar.

play.where: The time controller is the **Time** panel; the button below brings it into view, wherever you have put it.

steps.alt: The time controller under the map, with each track's position at current time marked by a square.

steps.title: Select tracks in the Outline
steps.text: Click **BLUE ONE** in the Outline, then Ctrl-click **RED ONE** to add it. The map outlines what is selected, and the tools offered change with the selection: with two tracks, **Closest approach** is on offer.
steps.keys: Move through the Outline and select from the keyboard; adding to the selection takes `Ctrl` too.

vscode.where: **Outline** is in the Debrief sidebar.
vscode.keys: `↑` and `↓` move through the Outline; `Enter` selects, `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` adds to the selection (`Cmd+Shift+Enter` on macOS).

play.where: **Outline** is a panel; the button below brings it into view, wherever you have put it.
play.keys: `Tab` moves through the Outline; `Enter` selects, `Ctrl+Enter` adds to the selection.

steps.alt: BLUE ONE and RED ONE selected on the map, the other tracks dimmed.

steps.title: Compare tracks in the Tote
steps.text: In the Tote, choose **BLUE ONE** as the primary and add **RED ONE**. Each row is a measure, worked out at current time: range, true bearing, relative bearing (`R` to port, `G` to starboard), angle on the bow, bearing rate, and each track's course, speed and depth. Move current time and they follow.
steps.keys: **Primary** and **Add** are lists: `Tab` to one, `↓` to choose. Or, on a track in the Outline, `Shift+F10` opens its menu: **Set as Tote primary**, **Add to Tote**.

vscode.where: **Tote** is below the time controller; it starts folded.

play.where: **Tote** is a panel; the button below brings it into view, wherever you have put it.

steps.alt: The Tote: a row for each measure, a column for BLUE ONE and one for RED ONE, with a thin line on the map between them.

steps.title: Read the narrative in the Timeline
steps.text: The Timeline lists BLUE ONE's, RED ONE's and exercise control's logs in one time order. Choose an entry: current time moves to it, and the entry is shown beside its track on the map. While playing, the list follows current time.
steps.keys: `↑` and `↓` move through the list; `Enter` chooses an entry; `/` searches.

vscode.where: **Timeline** is in the Debrief sidebar.

play.where: **Timeline** is a panel; the button below brings it into view, wherever you have put it.

steps.alt: The Timeline's entries in time order, the one at current time marked, and its text beside RED ONE on the map.

tours.title: Import and collate
tours.description: Import BLUE ONE's navigation log, see where each source has data, take the new data and choose which source supplies a period. About 8 minutes.

steps.title: Open a copy of serial 1
steps.text: A fresh copy of serial 1, titled *Serial 1: Import and collate*, with BLUE ONE's navigation log ready to import beside it: a fix every 10 s for part of the serial, as new data would arrive after an exercise. The sample itself never changes.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the button and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: The copy goes into a catalogue of its own, *Walkthrough: Import and collate*.

play.where: The copy is added to the plots under *Plot*, in the top bar.

steps.alt: The map of serial 1, BLUE ONE's track highlighted.

steps.title: Import the navigation log
steps.text: Import *blue-one-nav-log.rep*, a REP file. Debrief asks, for each track, whether it is plotted over the ground (OTG), each fix where it was logged, or by dead reckoning (DR); choose **Over the ground (OTG)**. The file is kept unchanged as a source, and the import is a plot of its own in the catalogue. A legacy Debrief .dpf plot is imported the same way.
steps.keys: In each question, `↓` chooses and `Enter` imports.

vscode.where: Your own files: **Import plot file (REP, .dpf, Word, PDF)…** on Catalogues' title bar.

play.where: The log comes with the sample: nothing is uploaded.

steps.alt: A REP file of fixes becoming a new item in the catalogue.

steps.title: See where each source has data
steps.text: In the catalogue, the log is marked **✦ New data**: imported after the plot, sharing a platform with it and with data in its period. **Coverage** shows each of the plot's tracks with a bar for every source of its data, the periods each covers filled in.
steps.keys: `Tab` moves through Coverage's tracks, bars and lists.

vscode.where: **Coverage** is below Catalogues; it starts folded.

play.where: **Catalogue** and **Coverage** are panels; the button below brings Coverage into view, wherever you have put it.

steps.alt: Coverage: BLUE ONE with two bars, the plot's own data and the navigation log's, overlapping for part of the serial.

steps.title: Take the new data
steps.text: **Take** brings the log's data into the plot as one step: BLUE ONE gains fixes where it had none, and WATCHER, a contact the plot had not seen, is added. Undo takes it back.
steps.keys: `Tab` to **Take** and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: **Take** is in Coverage; or **Take data into the open plot…** on the log's menu in Catalogues.

play.where: **Take** is beside the log in **Catalogue** and in **Coverage**.

steps.alt: BLUE ONE's track extended by the log's fixes, and WATCHER added.

steps.title: Choose a source for a period
steps.text: Where the plot and the log both have data for BLUE ONE, choose which supplies that period: the log's fixes are every 10 s, the plot's every minute. Pick the log in the period's list and press **Set**, or click its bar. One step, naming the item and the period.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the period's list, `↑` and `↓` to pick (nothing changes yet), then `Enter` or **Set**.

vscode.where: In **Coverage**, under BLUE ONE.

play.where: In **Coverage**, under BLUE ONE.

steps.alt: Coverage with the log chosen to supply the period where the two overlap.

tours.title: Tidy a track
tours.description: Remove GPS glitches, smooth a track, mark and label a fix, and shear a leg as in TMA. About 10 minutes.

steps.title: Open a copy of serial 1, with glitches
steps.text: A fresh copy of serial 1, titled *Serial 1: Tidy a track*. Three of RED ONE's fixes have been moved miles off its track, as GPS glitches would put them; the step that did it is in History, so it is never mistaken for real data. The sample itself never changes.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the button and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: The copy goes into a catalogue of its own, *Walkthrough: Tidy a track*.

play.where: The copy is added to the plots under *Plot*, in the top bar.

steps.alt: RED ONE's track with three spikes where its glitched fixes are.

steps.title: Remove the jumps
steps.text: A jump is a fix RED ONE could not have reached in time: faster than three times its median speed, and at least 10 kn. Select RED ONE and find its jumps: they are ringed on the map and listed, each ticked. Untick any that are real, then remove the rest, as one step.
steps.keys: `Space` ticks and unticks a jump in the list.

vscode.where: **Find and remove jumps…** is on RED ONE's menu in the Outline.
vscode.keys: `Enter` takes the threshold offered; in the list of jumps, `Space` ticks and unticks and `Enter` removes those ticked.

play.where: **Jumps…** is under *Track*, in the **Outline** panel.
play.keys: `Enter` on **Find** takes the threshold offered; `Tab` through the jumps, `Space` ticks and unticks, then `Enter` on **Remove**.

steps.alt: RED ONE with its three jumps ringed.

steps.title: Smooth the track
steps.text: Smoothing moves each fix to the average of itself and the fixes either side, over an odd number of fixes; the first and last stay where they are, and no time changes. Debrief shows the track as it would be, dashed, and how far fixes would move, before you apply it as one step.
steps.keys: Type the number of fixes and press `Enter`; then **Apply**.

vscode.where: **Smooth track…** is on the track's menu in the Outline.

play.where: **Smooth…** is under *Track*, in the **Outline** panel.

steps.alt: RED ONE and, dashed beside it, the track as smoothing would leave it.

steps.title: Mark and label a fix
steps.text: Give one fix a colour, a label or a comment of its own: the moment RED ONE turned, say. The fix list shows every fix with its time, position, course and speed; choose one, then its colour or **Label…**. Each change is one step, and the mark stays with its fix whatever else changes.
steps.keys: `↑` and `↓` move through the fix list; `Enter` chooses a fix.

vscode.where: **Fixes: colour, label or comment…** is on the track's menu in the Outline; or right-click a fix on the map.

play.where: **Fixes…** is under *Track*; or right-click a fix on the map.

steps.alt: One of RED ONE's fixes drawn in its own colour with a label beside it.

steps.title: Shear a leg, as in TMA
steps.text: Shear holds one end of a track and moves the other: every fix moves in proportion to its time from the held end, so a straight leg stays straight with a new course and speed. It is the drag analysts use most on TMA legs. Select BLUE ONE and drag the diamond beside its last fix; the map gives the new course and speed. Letting go is one step.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the diamond and use the arrow keys. Or shear by typing the course and speed made good.

vscode.where: **Shear track…** is on the track's menu in the Outline.

play.where: **Shear…** is under *Track*, in the **Outline** panel.

steps.alt: BLUE ONE's leg sheared: the start held, the end dragged by its diamond to a new position.

tours.title: Annotate and export a figure
tours.description: Draw an annotation, label the times on tracks, export the map as an image that traces to its plot, and find the plot again from the image. About 10 minutes.

steps.title: Open a copy of serial 1
steps.text: A fresh copy of serial 1, titled *Serial 1: Annotate and export a figure*. The sample itself never changes.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the button and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: The copy goes into a catalogue of its own, *Walkthrough: Annotate and export a figure*.

play.where: The copy is added to the plots under *Plot*, in the top bar.

steps.alt: The map of serial 1, ready to annotate.

steps.title: Draw an annotation
steps.text: On the map's toolbar choose **Area**, click each corner and double-click the last: the map gives ranges, bearings and the area as you draw. Name it in the form, such as *Search area*, and press **Add**. It is one step; drag a corner later to change it.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the map's toolbar and press `Enter` on **Area**; the arrow keys pan the map under the cross, `Space` places a corner, `Enter` finishes. Or add it by typing the positions.

vscode.where: The toolbar is on the map; **Add annotation…** is on the Outline's title bar.

play.where: The toolbar is on the map; **Add…** is under *Annotation*, in the **Outline** panel.

steps.alt: An area drawn on the map in amber, dashed and labelled Search area.

steps.title: Label the times on tracks
steps.text: Select BLUE ONE and RED ONE, then set their frequencies: labels every 10 min and arrows every 5 min, one step for both. The times sit beside each track on the clock's tens; zoomed out, they thin to round times, and the map says so.
steps.keys: Each of labels, symbols and arrows is a list: `↓` to choose, `Enter` for the next; or type an interval such as `90 s`.

vscode.where: **Frequencies: labels, symbols and arrows…** is on a track's menu in the Outline.
vscode.button: Set BLUE ONE's and RED ONE's frequencies

play.where: **Frequencies…** is under *Track*, in the **Outline** panel.
play.button: Set BLUE ONE's and RED ONE's frequencies

steps.alt: BLUE ONE and RED ONE labelled with their times every 10 minutes, with direction arrows.

steps.title: Export a traceable image
steps.text: Export the map as a PNG, as a 1600 × 900 slide. It is the map as you see it, labels where the map put them. The image carries an ID naming this plot and the exact step it shows: in its metadata, and in a small footer, such as `DBF-PTET-KG8R-B9EM-69`, for when Word or PowerPoint drops the metadata. Exporting is never a step.
steps.keys: Each choice is a list or a box to tick: `↓`, `Space`, `Enter`.

vscode.where: **Export image…** is the camera on the map's title bar.

play.where: **Export** is in the top bar; your browser saves the file.

steps.alt: The exported image: the map with the image's ID in its least busy corner.

steps.title: Find the image's source
steps.text: Change the plot, then find the image's source: type the ID from its corner (or choose the image file). Debrief opens the plot as it was when the image was exported, read-only, at the view and time exported. **Go to latest** returns to the plot as it is now.
steps.keys: Type the ID and press `Enter`; on the map, `Tab` to **Go to latest** and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: **Find source of image…** is on Catalogues' title bar menu.

play.where: Under **Find source of image**, in the top bar's *Export* menu.

steps.alt: The image's ID leading back to the plot, shown read-only at the step it was exported.

tours.title: Bearings and TMA
tours.description: BLUE ONE's towed array on RED ONE, in serial 1: keep a side of an ambiguous bearing, make a TMA solution from a period of cuts, drag it to fit, leave out a wild bearing and split it into legs. About 10 minutes.

steps.title: Open a copy of serial 1 and its bearings
steps.text: A fresh copy of serial 1, titled *Serial 1: Bearings and TMA*, with **Bearings** listing the cuts of BLUE ONE's towed array, drawn on the map in purple. A towed array cannot tell port from starboard, so each cut has two bearings, mirrored about BLUE ONE's course: two lines, the port one solid and the starboard one dashed, until you keep one. One cut has been turned 40° off, as a wild bearing would be; the step that did it is in History. The sample itself never changes.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the button and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: The copy goes into a catalogue of its own, *Walkthrough: Bearings and TMA*. **Bearings** is in the Debrief sidebar, after the Timeline.

play.where: The copy is added to the plots under *Plot*, in the top bar; the button brings the **Bearings** panel into view.

steps.alt: BLUE ONE's towed array cuts on the map, each a pair of lines: one solid to port, one dashed to starboard.

steps.title: Keep a side of an ambiguous bearing
steps.text: The button chooses the towed array's cut at 09:46Z and moves current time there, so the map draws it wider. BLUE ONE's Bow sonar is not ambiguous: its teal line at that time is at 235°. So keep the towed array's bearing that agrees, **Keep 236.3° (starboard)**, in Bearings, or click the cut's line on the map and keep it there. It is one step. **Next ambiguous** goes on to the next cut, and **Ambiguous bearings: keep port or starboard…** on the sensor's menu keeps one side for a whole period.
steps.keys: In Bearings' list, `Alt+↓` and `Alt+↑` go to the next and previous ambiguous cut; `Tab` to **Keep 236.3° (starboard)** and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: In **Bearings**, beside the list; or on the map.

play.where: In the **Bearings** panel, beside the list; or on the map. **Port…** and **Starboard…** under *Sensor*, in the **Outline** panel, keep a side for a period.

steps.alt: One towed-array cut's two lines, the one kept beside the Bow sonar's line at the same time.

steps.title: Make a first guess
steps.text: A solution is rooted in a period of one sensor's cuts, chosen in Bearings' list: click its first cut and Shift-click its last. The button chooses the towed array's cuts from 09:46Z to 12:00Z and opens **Make solution…**, the first guess: 10,000 yd (4.94 nmi) along the first cut's bearing, a course across it, 8 kn. Keep Debrief's defaults and press **Make solution**. Contact 1's solution is drawn on the map, and Bearings shows its residuals: each cut's bearing less the solution's. An RMS over 50° says the guess is far off. **Two clicks on the map instead** takes the first guess from a click on the first cut's line and one on the last's.
steps.keys: In the list, `Shift` with `↓` or `↑` extends the period; `Tab` to **Make solution…** and press `Enter`. The form takes the keyboard; `Enter` makes the solution.

vscode.where: In **Bearings**. **TMA solution from a sensor's cuts…**, in the Command Palette, takes you to the list.
vscode.button: Choose the period and open the first guess

play.where: In the **Bearings** panel.
play.button: Choose the period and open the first guess

steps.alt: The first guess, a straight solution heading away across the bearings, far from them.

steps.title: Drag the solution to fit
steps.text: The solution is a track, so its drags are a track's. Drag the diamond at its end on the map: its start stays where it is (a shear), and Bearings works the residuals and the RMS out again as you drag. Bring the calculated line through the dots: about 215° at 3 kn takes the RMS from over 50° to about 14°. Letting go is one step.
steps.keys: `Tab` to the diamond and use the arrow keys, `Shift` for bigger steps. Or shear by typing the course and speed made good, such as `215` and `3 kn`.

vscode.where: **Shear track…** is on the solution's menu in the Outline.

play.where: **Shear…** is under *Track*, in the **Outline** panel.

steps.alt: The solution sheared about its start, nearer the bearings, with its residuals in Bearings.

steps.title: Leave out a wild bearing
steps.text: One residual lies far from the rest: the cut at 11:12Z, some 40° off where its neighbours are near 0°. The button chooses it in Bearings' list. Leave it out of the RMS: press `Space`, or click its tick box. It is one step, and the RMS falls; the cut is still listed, struck through. `Space` again, or Undo, counts it again.
steps.keys: In Bearings' list, `↑` and `↓` to the cut, then `Space`; or `Tab` to **Leave this cut out of the RMS** and press `Enter`.

vscode.where: In **Bearings**, beside the list.
vscode.button: Choose the cut with the largest residual

play.where: In the **Bearings** panel.
play.button: Choose the cut with the largest residual

steps.alt: The residuals beneath the bearings, one dot far from the others, left out as a dotted ring.

steps.title: Split into legs and drag one
steps.text: No straight leg fits RED ONE: the residuals climb until 10:32Z and fall after the gap, because it turned there. The button chooses the cut at 10:38Z; press **Split into legs at 10:38:00Z**. It is one step, and the solution is still one track. Then choose **This leg** on the map, click the first leg and drag its end: about 285° at 4 kn brings its residuals down, and the second leg stays where it is. The step is done once a leg is dragged.
steps.keys: In Bearings' list, `↑` and `↓` to the cut, `Tab` to **Split into legs at …** and press `Enter`. On the map, **This leg** is a button, and the diamonds drag the leg current time is in: `Enter` on a cut in the list moves current time to it.

vscode.where: In **Bearings**, beside the list. **Split TMA solution into legs at current time** is on the solution's menu in the Outline.

play.where: In the **Bearings** panel; **This leg** is on the map, under *What changes*.

steps.alt: The solution in two legs joined at 10:38Z, the first dragged to a new course, the second where it was.
